item.title: Blocchiamo tutto! Ethics, Subjectivity and the Crisis of Political Forms in Italian Gaza Protests
item.description:
Introduction

The global movement in solidarity with Palestine was one of the largest cycles of political mobilisation in recent years. Across different national contexts, millions of people have taken part in demonstrations, occupations, strikes, and campaigns against the genocide in Gaza, bringing into political action a younger generation for whom these protests represented a first experience of collective mobilisation. Historically characterised by deeply rooted forms of solidarity with Palestine, Italy has witnessed a sustained wave of mobilisation since October 2023, involving workplaces, universities, schools, and public squares. A qualitative leap occurred in late September and early October 2025, beginning with the social strike of 22 September and culminating in a sequence of strikes and mass demonstrations that brought together an unusually heterogeneous social composition. The strike was termed ‘social’ since it blocked the circulation of goods and it involved those lacking the formal right to strike. Today, the movement is known with its slogan blocchiamo tutto! [block everything!], that refers to the occupation of key infrastructural hubs. The idea that the strike must adapt to capitalist restructuring beyond the confines of the workplaces was developed by Antonio Negri in the Nineties. The growing integration of the spheres of production and circulation redefined the terrain of struggle, shifting it from the factory to the metropolis.
After the Global Sumud Flotilla sailed under the constant threat of being intercepted by Israel, the social strike of 22 September mobilised more than eighty pickets, 65 protests in squares across the country. The even larger strike of October 3rd — the first to be jointly called by mainstream (CGIL - Confederazione Generale Italiana del Lavoro) and grassroots unions (CUB - Confederazione Unitaria di Base; SGB - Sindacato Generale di Base; USB - Unione Sindacale di Base; Cobas - Comitati di Base) — more than one hundred demonstrations across Italy, with over two million people taking part in protests nationwide. Activists blocked motorway junctions in Bologna, Rome, and Milan; port terminals in Livorno and Naples; railway stations in Cagliari, Florence, and Perugia; and airports in Florence and Pisa. The cycle of mobilisation reached its peak with the national demonstration in Rome on the 4th of October, which brought one million people onto the streets. Universities, which since the beginning of the movement in solidarity with Palestine in October 2023 had been among the principal sites of organisation and protest in Italy, assumed a relatively secondary role during the extraordinary weeks of mobilisation analysed here. During these weeks, the epicentre of mobilisation shifted, to the strategic nodes of circulation, with universities serving primarily as organisational hubs and departure points for local demonstrations. After the 4th of October, however, universities once again became central. As young people sought to relaunch the protest from their own places of life and study, occupations and actions aimed at disrupting the normal functioning of universities once again spread across the country. The extraordinary scale of participation and the heterogeneity of the actors involved in the protest were connected to classical repertoires of labour conflict and workplace mobilisation that disrupted production in order to oppose the genocide. At the same time, participation and political activation were often articulated through ethical commitments and opinion-based forms of engagement. Rather than constituting separate logics, these dimensions were deeply intertwined, challenging conventional political categories. These novel elements led us to organise a co-research to understand emerging forms of political organisation and subjectivation. Our motivation was not simply sociological curiosity. Rather, we sought to read between the lines of the moral and ethical mobilisation that brought masses of young people back into the streets on a scale not seen for more than a decade. While we are aware that these forms of political activation may easily slide into individualism, we cannot fail to recognise their importance as processes of counter-subjectivation that expressed unprecedented levels of radicality. What forms of organisation and subjectivation can subvert neoliberal individualism and isolation, creating spaces of collective politicisation and enabling insurrection to endure, reproduce itself, and expand?

1. The Politics of Co-research

Our political methodology comes from the tradition of operaismo and our point of departure is the figure of Romano Alquati, who played a decisive role in conducting the famous co-researches in the large Fordist factories of northern Italy during the Seventies (Wright 2021, 51–67). While reflecting on university and education in the Seventies, Alquati noted some historical changes. In this context, education — understood as part of the apparatus of capital’s reproduction — served “to manipulate workers’ subjectivity (as workers and citizens) toward the needs of businesses and capitalist accumulation” (Alquati 1976, 55). From these reflections, Alquati provided a definition of formation: “the embodiment within living labour, in the living labour power, of the social knowledge” (Alquati 1978, 56). Thinking of formation as knowledge embodied in living labour — living knowledge — draws attention to the fact that general social knowledge must always be embodied in concrete subjectivity, in the concrete body of the student-worker (Roggero 2011, 61–85). Co-research is the organisation of an alternative process of formation: organise the embodiment of social knowledge in living labour in an antagonistic and alternative way. We believe that the production of (counter-)subjectivity is not simply a discursive or theoretical process. Rather, it is deeply rooted in struggle and political organisation. Subjectivities are shaped as much by material practices as by discourse. In his discussion with another key figure of early Operaismo, Raniero Panzieri, Alquati distinguished workers’ inquiry from co-research precisely on this political ground. Panzieri believed that the sociological rigour of the workers’ inquiry could be both criticised and appropriated, much as Marx engaged with political economy. This meant recognising its methodological precision, scientific coherence and partial truths (Panzieri 1965, 67-76). Alquati, by contrast, emphasises the immediate political character of co-research. For him, co-research entails the production of knowledge and, simultaneously, the self-organisation of the class; it is linked to the “production, over time, of (counter)-subjects” (Alquati 1994, 21). In Panzieri’s framework, workers’ inquiry functions primarily as a tool for gathering knowledge about the condition of the working class, which can then be politically mobilised by trade unions and parties (Chicchi & Cominu 2013, 120–38). For Alquati, however, co-research has neither a clear beginning nor a clear end; it is an “open processuality”. As he writes: “[…] All in all, co-research may be thought as something permanent and endless […] Co-research begins with a certain hypothesis on reality directed toward its transformation, giving form to new hypothesis of further transformation, permanent, continuous, toward certain constitutive and creative final ends” (Alquati 1993, 38). The end of co-research is therefore political organisation. Alquati’s argument suggests that co-research produces struggles, political organisation and counter-subjectivity. This is necessarily a collective process: the prefix co-emphasises its collective dimension. Co-research not only abolishes the distinction between researchers and the subjects of research; it is itself a “collective construction” that “provokes a change in one’s own social practices” (Sacchetto, Armano and Wright 2013). Organisation, struggle and subjectivity are the defining elements of co-research. Its emphasis on collective knowledge production and formation is an emphasis on understanding and organising the conditions through which subjectivity can become antagonistic. This process is no separated from concrete political organisation. The enigma of co-research lies precisely here: it cannot simply be theorised; it must be practised — by talking with people, attempting to organise them, failing, and trying again. When the mobilisations against the genocide erupted and rapidly escalated into an unexpected mass movement, we decided that the first task was to investigate the conditions that had made the emergence of these new revolutionary subjectivities possible. In the spirit of co-research, we sought to understand the processes of counter-subjectivation at work within the mobilisations, hoping that they represented not an isolated event but the concrete manifestation of a new form of revolutionary politics.

2 Within and Against Neoliberal Subjectivity. The Subversive Potential of Indignation

Organised within a university collective, composed primarily of students and PhD candidates, we participated in the autumn mobilisations from our own positionality of students, young researchers, and political militants. This reflects the positionality of our co-research. We conducted a series of qualitative interviews with young people involved in the autumn 2025 protest cycle. Roughly, participants were between 19 and 25 years old, and for the vast majority of the interviewees these protests represented their first significant experience of political mobilisation. The first interviews were conducted directly at demonstrations, either during the protests or immediately afterwards. Further interviews were carried out in the following days, many of them in universities occupied as part of the mobilisation, particularly in the Faculties of Biological Sciences, Physics, and Political Science. The hypotheses that emerged from this first phase of the inquiry gave rise to a second phase of co-research, which is still ongoing, and it explores the forms of political engagement that (do not) persisted beyond the weeks of protest.

2.1 Blocking Everything is a Bodily Necessity

During the widespread demonstrations, we witnessed millions of people taking over the street to block everything. As G. recalls: “At the beginning, it all started with a picket. It was really the first few days, I mean, on the first night [at the occupied university] there were ten of us, which was already a good number. And then, from there, we started to let more and more people in [inside the occupied university], until the flotilla was actually blocked: we had already anticipated that. They block the flotilla, we block everything, we occupy the university. So, once that happened, we found ourselves really crowded in here” (Interview with G.). Places identified as parts of the logistical and economic infrastructure, through which the Italian State and Meloni’s government is complicit in the genocide in Gaza, were blockaded through occupations, pickets, and marches. Universities were not spared by protests, since they were perceived as a cog in the machine of genocide: they were blocked and occupied precisely like streets and train stations. B. argues: “Our government’s lack of response makes you angry, it makes you feel helpless, perhaps this is the only way to show that I personally have a voice and actually have the opportunity to express my disagreement with the government” (Interview with B.). Blocking the movement of people and goods, within and beyond traditional union practices such as strikes and picketing, showed disagreement with the Italian government. However, for some of those participating in the movement, any possibility for a democratic and representative mediation was already surpassed. As the quote by B. shows, the direct action of blocking everything is determined by the feeling that mediation has already failed, and that those in power have no intention of listening. In this sense, the blocchiamo tutto!’s overflowing moments expressed a total and irreconcilable political contrapposition with Meloni’s government. In fact, as C. expresses: “I want to give physical, corporeal vent to the disgust that is happening; I want to say no with all my strength” (Interview with C.). Indeed, the practices of blocchiamo tutto! has a bodily dimension, expressed as an immediate corporeal demonstration of dissent. In last analysis, these dynamics highlight a crucial shift: direct action takes the form of such a genuine urgency that the temporality of immediate action - the here and now - replaces the long temporality of organizational structuring and internal debate within the movement. This is explicitly underlined by A.: “What I’m always a little afraid of is that we waste too much time talking and not enough action. Recently, we’ve seen the opposite: we’re acting. In short, I feel… I’m happy with the situation of the last few weeks […]. It’s clear that there must be moments of discussion, certainly, but we’re truly in a moment where even tomorrow we don’t know what will happen” (Interview with A.). In the face of tomorrow’s uncertainty, there emerges a preference of public demonstration over those of decision-making or assembly. In other words, taking over the streets was chosen instead of the traditional places of both radical and moderate left-wing politics. In this context, traditional forms of organisation, assemblies, and discussions, were passed over by this prioritization of direct action. This point raises the issue of the movement’s ability to create institutions that can ensure the continuity of the insurrectionary moment. While the blocchiamo tutto! movement surpassed traditional forms of organization; it did not invent new ones.

2.2 The Ethical Dimension, Indignation and Ambiguities of Neoliberal Subjectivation

When it comes to retrace the motivations that drove people to mobilize, a sense of impotence and horror towards the reality of the genocide is by far one of the most commonly recorded. As L. states: “Demonstrating is perhaps the only truly strong signal we can send to the population, and one that those who govern us fear the most. Therefore, it is the first move, it is the first step, and it is right that it should be so because it channels an unsustainable indignation” (Interview with L.). The ethical and humanitarian dimension played a pivotal role too. The escalation of violence in Palestine and the government’s indifference were felt as an unbearable violation of universal human values. Perceiving oneself as part of a shared humanity, outraged by the cynical attitude of those in power, was often a driving force, like in the case of G., interviewed during the national demonstration in Rome on October the 4th: “I started to feel the need to take to the streets, let’s say for a classic reason: because it’s an inhuman thing. I, as a human being, I mean…” (Interview with G.). Thus, taking to the streets was felt as a way of reaffirming the protestors’ own sense of humanity too, stained by their government’s inaction. Demonstrating was often conceived as a way of marking a difference from all those complicit in the genocide in Palestine, a way of being and feeling better: “Nobody does anything, like the people who have power in their hands, you know. Then also I feel sad because, I mean, I put myself in their shoes. Watching the videos makes me feel sick. At least, after protesting, I feel good with myself, with my conscience, because I know that I did the little I could do” (Interview with G.). The ethical ground became the affective basis on which an atomised plurality could recompose itself through an internal torsion of neoliberal subjectivation. In Individu et communauté chez Spinoza (1988), Alexandre Matheron reads this dynamic as an imitative process. Indignation is the hatred that stems from the impossibility of ignoring the suffering inflicted on someone we perceive as sharing a common nature with us. In the face of the scandal of violence, indignation spreads and reinforces itself, as said, through a mechanism of imitation: since it is perceived as universally shared, the hatred directed at those responsible multiplies, ultimately breaking the isolation imposed by fear and unifying the multitude. It is precisely this affect that Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri define “the raw material of revolt” (2009, p. 236), the most effective tool through which singularities discover the possibility of acting against oppression. Indignation, they argue, is precisely the “ground zero” where a collective polarisation begins, yet taking the shape of a “singular phenomenon, in response to a specific […] violation” (Hardt & Negri, 2009, p. 236). The same movement is at work in our case: indignation towards the genocide opened a fracture in the individualistic subjectivation, prompting a collective response and a bodily necessity to reject the current state of things. As members of a shared humanity outraged by genocide, protestors perceived Palestinians as ‘like them’ and saw their own government as complicit with Israel , that is, as an equally legitimate object of indignation. The interview with B. is the best way to see how this dynamic of indignation was embodied by young protestors: “It’s literally a necessity, the incarnation of a feeling of indignation that doesn’t want to stay that way, it wants to become […] a struggle for change. The demonstrations and the squares for Palestine […] channel precisely a feeling of deep indignation towards the Italian government, towards Italian institutions, towards universities, towards the political class that governs Italy, towards Italian arms companies, towards the system we’re all part of, that behaves in a shameful way” (Interview with B.). However, this process bears the signs of the individualistic and atomised subjectivation engendered by neoliberalism. The protestors were mainly focused on their personal sphere of action and the drive to be better risks appearing merely self-exculpatory. Yet this affirmation of difference did not remain confined within the sphere of individual discipline: the potentia of unsustainable indignation pressed against and ultimately cracked open the limits of neoliberal forms of life, assuming a collective shape. Thus, a structural ambiguity defines neoliberal subjectivity in this context. Indignation, ethical rejection and individual action are the core of its agency, normally harmless to the status quo since confined within an atomised landscape of separate individuals, where collective actors are perceived as no longer effective. Therefore, the response to genocide could only be individual, and yet it unfolded within a mass dimension: one could even say, paradoxical as this may seem, that people participated as individuals in a collective movement.
Indignation thus became, disjunctively, both the trace of capital and the driving force of a multitude of singularities, willing to call the government to account of its complicity and to show themselves as genuinely different: “In my opinion people are getting tired and we’ve finally reached the peak of all this. What we see in government is a disgrace, we’re ashamed of our government and I feel that people want to change” (Interview with S.). Indeed, striving to become “the best version of oneself” — a recurring mantra of neoliberal self-entrepreneurship and self-optimisation — was a common aspiration among young protesters, but it was not confined within the sphere of personal valorisation or success: it was considered as intrinsically political and embedded in the social interaction with other people. In this perspective, political action must be situated within a wider ethical orientation that could also encompass ecological choices, veganism, and other everyday practices extending across the different contexts in which one lives and works. In our context, not showing one’s own support for Palestine during everyday life, like boycotting Israeli products, was felt as an act of complicity. As A. says in their interview: “All those that make up this community are complicit in some way, if they don’t do something, if they don’t act within the possibilities they have” (Interview with A.). Accordingly, small and concrete actions, within the boundaries of what can be done in one’s daily life, are usually considered more effective and useful than being part of an organised context oriented towards broader projects. The immediacy of a small and personal result – not being a passive part of oppression dynamics – seems to be preferred to the longer struggle for a more general one – the abolition of oppression dynamics themselves. Nevertheless, this is not a mere retreat into the private. The everyday refusal of complicity is already lived as political; yet indignation has also driven people into the streets, in a peculiar form of collective participation. What the squares for Palestine reveal, then, is precisely the ambiguity of this neoliberal subjectivity, which seems to compose itself through, rather than against, its proper atomisation, thus converting indignation and the drive to ‘do one’s part’ into a shared potentia. Whether this affective recomposition can outlast the dispersal back into individual life – whether it can turn the immediacy of indignation into the duration of struggle – remains the open and decisive question.

2.3 The political enigma: Material Infrastructure, Symbolic Identification

Many interviews suggest that the main impulse behind mobilizations, and the reasons for the qualitative leap of those weeks, converge into two closely connected factors: (i) the general strike and the logistical support provided by the various organizational infrastructures (material factor); (ii) the strong sense of self-identification and reflection in the Global Sumud Flotilla initiative (symbolic factor). As far as the first point is concerned, D., G., and A argue: “The first time I went out into the streets for Palestine was with the strike, with the general strike” (Interview with D.). “I think that during this period the trade unions have regained some of the leading role in organising strikes that they may have lost in recent years” (Interview with G.). “Workers’ strikes are much more important because, in my opinion, they have far more power than we do” (Interview with A.). The general strike is perceived as the only means capable of mobilising people and giving materiality and concreteness to the slogan: blocchiamo tutto! While we cannot deny the role played by material infrastructure in building mass mobilisation, we need to deepen the subjective component of this process. To grasp this dimension, we need to turn the analysis to the symbolic and catalysing role of the Global Sumud Flotilla. Around this, the interviews reveal its absolute importance, although for different and sometimes even opposed reasons. For M., the Flotilla appears as an event capable of condensing hope, efficacy and identification: “Who knows if it’s true or not… that with all the media attention focused on the flotilla, the Israeli army was completely preoccupied with it, and so people in Gaza were able to go fishing. If we’ve managed to achieve something like this through demonstrations alone – to help the people there survive a little longer – then in my view we’ve already won. That in itself is the foundation of everything” (Interview with M.).

A more detached tone emerges in those accounts that stress how the boarding of the Flotilla — and the media attention it generated — brought in the streets people that remained silent on the Palestinian cause until then. Such accounts raise the question of why the mobilization expanded so dramatically only at this particular moment, after months of the Palestinian people’s daily suffering. A.’s interview points in this direction when emphasizing the presence of many new participants in the Rome demonstration: “In Rome we saw a million people. A lot of them were definitely new — like, last year maybe they’d never have taken part, two years ago they wouldn’t even have imagined getting involved in this cause — and some of that turnout came down to the Global Sumud Flotilla too, which created all that media attention” (Interview with A.). This reading certainly captures something real. Yet it is precisely by remaining within the tensions opened that a broader political question appears. Rather than turning the belatedness or partiality of this political activation into the object of a moral critique (why have you mobilized only now?), we should ask why this occurred and what this ambivalent form of solidarity can become. In fact, what matters politically is whether this initial impulse can be displaced from a merely moral response into a more concrete form of political commitment: one that recognizes the asymmetry of power relations, questions the positionality from which one speaks and reconnects that position to the responsibilities state and capital. In this regard, this extract from the interview with G. is particularly telling: “If, from my position, I can afford to live a comfortable, peaceful life, to choose a profession, a circle of friends, then this must be permitted everywhere — and even more so if this lack of permission, as in the case of the Palestinian territories, is made worse by policies coming from my own state” (Interview with G.).

This is why, out of a hundred criticisms of privilege, we prefer even a genuine, albeit dirty, challenge to it: we say dirty to emphasize the contradictory aspects that every real movement inevitably contains and involves. In the case of the Flotilla, we have seen how an action that, on the surface, might have been dismissed as mere humanitarianism very quickly became a symbol of genuine solidarity between peoples capable of exerting influence, instilling courage and expanding the ranks of those engaged in the struggle. As political militants, we must therefore remember that critique is not external to the world it addresses but is bound up with the process of transforming it.

Conclusion

Blocchiamo tutto! reopened the question of how collective political action is constituted today. The strength of the blockade lay in its immediacy. Yet this immediacy was accompanied by a relative absence of spaces for discussion and organisation (Section 2.1). Neoliberal forms of subjectivation, visible in these protests, are marked by an intrinsic ambivalence that constituted both the principal strength and the principal limitation of the autumn 2025 mobilisations. While the neoliberal imperative to ‘become the best version of oneself’ can produce an ethical commitment that becomes politically conflictual, it can also reproduce forms of individualisation that foreclose the construction of a shared political horizon (Section 2.2). As political militants, we do not look for pure forms of class struggle, rejecting whatever fails to correspond to the categories of our theoretical textbooks (Section 2.3). Therefore, while deliberately recognising the political potential of these ambiguous forms of subjectivation, we acknowledge how, today, in the summer of 2026, blocchiamo tutto! is already a pale memory: people keep dying in Gaza and the everyday reproduction of capital and the state in Italy appears to continue undisturbed. Moreover, the ongoing second phase of our co-research shows that a widespread sense of powerlessness and disillusionment has come to characterise many of those who took part in the protests. What we believe is politically important to recognise, to overcome these limitations, is that, unlike many emancipatory movements in history, direct actions, occupations and blockades were not accompanied by an expansion of democratic participation. Blocchiamo tutto! failed to build durable forms of organisation. The ambivalent processes of counter-subjectivation described in this article were gradually reabsorbed into people’s everyday lives, rather than being consolidated within enduring organisational forms. The question on what form of organisation can be suitable for our time remains open. Nevertheless, we do believe that it is necessary to raise the problem of endurance — how struggles can achieve continuity and sedimentation — that leads Michael Hardt and Antonio Negri to pose the question of institutions, a concept that may help us think through the dilemmas of the present conjuncture (2009, 2017). For Hardt and Negri, institutions preserve and deepen the rupture opened by insurrection, giving organisation and stability to its achievements. We refer, with Hardt and Negri, to autonomous forms of institutionality that differ both from state institutions and from the traditional organisational forms of the revolutionary movement. Emerging from processes of class self-organisation, they operate as a counterpower to capitalist and state command. “To be a communist means […] to build the institutions of the common” (Negri 2023, 136): to create the conditions through which a collective power becomes capable of reproducing itself, expanding its capacities, and giving continuity to its own practice of liberation. We are aware that there is an abyss between what we have called neoliberal subjectivity and autonomous institutions. Nevertheless, the autumn mobilisations offer an important clue: the unequivocal rejection of genocide and war expressed by the young people who took part in them. It is precisely within the ambivalences of these forms of subjectivation, rather than in the search for pure political subjects or more traditional forms of class struggle, that co-research can identify the conditions of possibility for building autonomous forms of struggle capable of enduring.
